frase_gancho.texto: A turquoise mosaic on shell, found in a bag among the roof beams.

puente_narrativo.texto: From jewelry we move on to more vessels in human form. Look for seated clay figures, their bodies painted red and black and their heads rising above the rim, men and women alike.

guion_corto.texto: More than one hundred seventy tiny stones cover this pendant. They are turquoise tesserae, glued one by one onto a seashell. A piece of leather, tied between the holes in the shell, completes the form, and together they imitate the body and head of a turtle. Below, a piece of bone serves as the tail. Among the turquoise there are also fragments of hematite, a red mineral, and a small rectangle of copper. The pendant hangs from a bead string, a strand of shell and stone beads almost one meter long. It comes from Paquimé, in Chihuahua, from the time of its greatest splendor, between the years one thousand two hundred and one thousand four hundred fifty. It was found by the team of the archaeologist Charles Di Peso, inside a cotton bag, among the roof beams of a room.

guion_largo.texto:
Among the roof beams of a room in Paquimé, a cotton bag was left behind. Inside were two necklaces, and from one of them hung this turtle. More than five centuries later, it was found by the team of Charles Di Peso, who excavated the city between 1958 and 1961. That campaign was the most important ever carried out at the site.

The room was part of a sector that archaeologists call the House of the Well. In that same unit, more than three million pieces of seashell appeared. For the museum, that figure shows how important the shell industry was in the city. The raw material came from far away: according to studies, from the coasts of the Gulf of California. In other rooms of Paquimé, thousands of finished ornaments were counted, such as beads, pendants and tesserae.

Now notice the color. Turquoise does not occur naturally in Chihuahua. A study by INAH archaeologists indicates that the turquoise worked in Paquimé was imported from mines in New Mexico, in the southwestern United States. You have already seen it on this tour: in the Mixtec skull in the Oaxaca Hall, in the mosaic disk from Tula, and in the [Malinaltepec Mask](mna_s10_mascara_malinaltepec). It has been proposed that a good part of the turquoise in Mesoamerica came from the north, and that Paquimé was a stopping point along that route. Other specialists point out that turquoise was not abundant in the city itself. That is why a pendant almost covered with it must have been a piece of great value.

And why a turtle? The museum says only that the shell and the leather, joined together, imitate the body and head of the animal. What it meant to the person who wore it, we do not know. In other places the turtle carried many meanings. The Maya imagined the earth as the back of a turtle, and the Mimbres potters of the southwestern United States painted turtles on their bowls around the year one thousand. In Paquimé, the meaning remains open.

Look also at the necklace, which is part of the piece. The first thirty centimeters of the bead string have two pairs of threads with reddish and turquoise beads. In the center there is a round shell disk with a few turquoise tesserae. The longer stretch is made up mostly of shell beads, many of them reddish, and a few of green stone.

Paquimé had another turtle. The museum holds a copper bell in that shape, which appeared in one of the city’s ball courts. It is hollow and was made with the lost-wax technique, the same one you saw in the bells in the West Hall. The tail works as a ring, and for that reason it is thought to have been hung. Two turtles in a single city: one of shell and turquoise, the other of metal.

Di Peso thought that merchants from Mesoamerica founded Paquimé to control trade between the Southwest and the south. It is an idea that is much debated today. What pieces like this one do show is a city connected to distant mines and coasts.

Before moving on, think about everything that traveled to make a single ornament: the shell from the sea, the turquoise from a distant mine, and the rest of the materials. Paquimé lies in the middle of the desert, and yet in this jewel there is room for a map of roads.

texto: Count the turquoise tesserae and imagine each one glued by hand onto the shell
Find the little piece of bone that serves as the turtle’s tail
Follow the bead string: where do the beads change in color and shape?

texto.Material: Seashell, leather, more than 170 turquoise tesserae, hematite, copper and bone, with a bead string of shell and slate beads
texto.Origin: House of the Well (Room 9-C), Paquimé, Chihuahua (excavations of Charles Di Peso)

texto.pregunta: Myth: Paquimé was only a stopping point along the road, where turquoise and shell simply passed through.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The city also worked those materials: in a single unit, more than three million pieces of shell were found, a sign of a true industry. Paquimé did not just receive goods, it also transformed them.
